FOREWORD 


"This Indian Standard (Second Revision) was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft finalized 
by the Water Quality Sectional Committee had been approved by the Chemical Division Council. 


Phosphorus is present in natural water and waste waters mostly in the form of phosphates. These can be classified 
into ortho-phosphates, condensed phosphates (pyro, meta and other poly phosphates) and organically bound 
phosphates. They are present in solution, in particles or detritus or in the bodies of aquatic organisms. 


Variety of sources give rise to various types of phosphates. Orthophosphates in small amounts or certain condensed 
phosphates are added to water supplies while treatment. Phosphates in larger quantities may be added during 
the process of laundering or other cleaning. Phosphates are extensively used for the treatment of boiler water. 
Orthophosphates used as fertilisers in agricultural or residential cultivated land are carried to surface waters with 
storm runoff and in relatively smaller amounts with melting snow. Organic phosphates are formed primarily by 
biological processes. They are contributed to sewage by body wastes and food residues and also may be formed 
from orthophosphates in biological treatment process or by receiving water biota. 


This standard was first revised in 1988. In the first revision of the standard, the following two methods for 
determination of phosphorus, were given: 


a) Vanadomolybdo - phosphoric acid method; and 
b) Stannous chloride method. 
In this second revision the following modifications have been incorporated: 


1) This standard has been renumbered as Part 31/Sec 1 as other sections will be developed for instrument 
based methods; 


2) Ascorbic acid method has been added; and 


3) Persulphate method for simultaneous determination of total nitrogen and total phosphorus has been 
added. 


This section of Part 31 covers determination of phosphorous by vanadomolybdo-phosphoric acid, stannous 
chloride, ascorbic acid and persulphate method. Section 2 of Part 31 specifies flow injection analysis (FIA) 
methods for the determination of orthophosphate in the mass concentration range from 0.01 mg/l to 1.0 mg/l (P), 
and total phosphorus by manual digestion in the mass concentration range from 0.1 mg/l to 10 mg/l (P). Section 3 
of Part 31 specifies continuous flow analysis (CFA) methods for the determination of orthophosphate in the mass 
concentration range from 0.01 mg/l to 1.00 mg/l P, and total phosphorus in the mass concentration range from 
0.10 mg/l to 10.0 mg/l P. 


In the preparation ofthis standard, considerable assistance has been derived from the method no 4500 P of standard 
methods for the examination of water and wastewaterl, published by the American Public Health Association, 
Washington, USA, 23nd Edition, 2017. 


In reporting the result of a test or analysis made in accordance with this standard, if the final value, observed or 
calculated, is to be rounded off, it shall be done in accordance with IS 2 : 2022 “Rules for rounding off numerical 
values ( second revision )’. 


IS 3025 (Part 31/Sec 1): 2022 


Indian Standard 


METHODS OF SAMPLING AND TEST 
(PHYSICAL AND CHEMICAL) 
FOR WATER AND WASTEWATER 


PART 31 PHOSPHORUS 


Section 1 Determination by vanadomolybdo-phosphoric acid, stannous chloride, 
ascorbic acid and persulphate method 


( Second Revision ) 


1SCOPE 


This standard (Part 31/Sec 1) prescribes four methods 
for determination of phosphorus, namely: 


a) Vanadomolybdo-phosphoric acid method; 
b) Stannous chloride method; 
с) Ascorbic acid method; and 


d) Persulphatemethodforsimultaneous determination 
of total nitrogen and total phosphorus. 


2SAMPLING AND STORAGE 


2.1 In order to differentiate between the dissolved 
forms of phosphorus, filter the sample immediately 
after collecting it. Preserve the sample by freezing it 
at or below — 10 °C. In few cases, 40 mg/l of mercuric 
chloride may be added to the samples, particularly 
when they are stored for a long period of time before 
the analysis. 


CAUTION — As mercuric chloride is hazardous, care must be 
taken for its disposal. 


2.2 Use of mercuric chloride is not encouraged. Use 
of acid or chloroform (СНСІ,) as a preservative is not 
recommended when different forms of phosphorus are 
to be determined. To determine the total phosphorus, 
add sulphuric acid or hydrochloric acid at pH « 2 and 
cool it to 4 ?C or freeze it without any additions. 


2.3 Samples that contain low concentrations of 
phosphorus should not be stored in plastic bottles 
unless kept in a frozen state because phosphates can be 
absorbed on the walls of the plastic bottles. 


2.4 Rinse all the glass containers by using dilute 
hydrochloric acid (HCI) and further rinse it several times 
with reagent water. Never use commercial detergents 
that contain phosphate for cleaning glassware that is 
to be used in analysis of phosphate. More strenuous 
cleaning techniques may be used. 


3 PRELIMINARY DIGESTION STEPS 


3.1 Phosphorus analysis involves the conversion of 
phosphorus present in water in different forms to 
dissolved orthophosphate which is then estimated 
calorimetrically. 


3.1.1 For Acid Hydrolysable Phosphates 


To a sample of 100 ml volume or to a part of it which 
is diluted to 100 ml, phenolphthalein indicator solution 
0.05 ml (1 drop) is added. Add strong acid solution 
drop wise, in case the red colour appears more acid 
is added to discharge the red colour. Again add 1 ml 
of acid and further boil the solution gently for about 
90 min. Add distilled water in order to keep the volume 
between 25 and 50 ml. Alternatively, heat the solution 
for 30 min in an autoclave or by using pressure cooker 
at 98 to137 kPa. Cool the solution and neutralize it to a 
faint pink colour by using sodium hydroxide solution. 
Restore it in 100 ml volumetric flask by making up the 
volume using distilled water. 


3.1.2 For Total Phosphorus 


3.1.2.1 Perchloric acid digestion 


This 1s used for digestion of organic phosphorus and 
samples of sediment and organic bound phosphorus 
compounds. Take the sample that contains the desired 
amount of phosphorus in a 125 ml ErlenMeyer flask. 
Acidify the sample using concentrated nitric acid 
(HNO,) to methyl orange, and then further add 5 ml 
concentrated HNO, and evaporate on a steam bath or 
hot plate to 15 to 20 ml. Add 10 ml of each concentrated 
nitric acid and perchloric acid to a conical flask of 
125 ml capacity by cooling it between the addition of 
concentrated nitric acid and perchloric acid. Add some 
boiling chips and heat it on a hot plate. Further, gently 
evaporate till dense white fumes of perchloric acid 
appears. In case the solution is not clear, cover the neck 
of the flask with a watch glass and keep the solution 


IS 3025 (Part 31/Sec 1): 2022 


boiling till it is clear. If required, 10 ml concentrated 
nitric acid is added, in order to ease oxidation. Cool 
the digested solution and then add 1 drop of aqueous 
phenolphthalein solution. Add 6 N sodium hydroxide 
solution till the colour of the solution turns pink. As 
per the requirement, filter the neutralized solution and 
wash filter using distilled water. Make the volume up to 
100 ml with distilled water. 


3.1.2.2 Sulphuric acid —nitric acid digestion 


Ina micro Kjeldahl flask, sample containing phosphorus 
(as determined by colorimetric method) in desired 
amount is measured. Add 5 ml of concentrated nitric 
acid and 1 ml of concentrated sulphuric acid. Digest the 
solution to a volume of 1 ml and continue till solution 
becomes colourless in order to remove nitric acid. 
Cool the solution and add to it approximately 20 ml 
of distilled water, phenolphthalein indicator 0.05 ml 
(1 drop) and 1 N sodium hydroxide solution in a 
quantity that is required to produce a faint pink tinge. 
Into a 100 ml volumetric flask, transfer the neutralized 
solution and filter it if required so as to remove 
particulate material or any kind of turbidity. Sample 
volume to 100 ml is adjusted by using distilled water. 


3.1.2.3 Persulphate digestion method 


Take 50 ml or a suitable proportion of sample. Add 
phenolphthalein indicator solution (0.05 ml) to it. If 
red colour appears, sulphuric acid solution is added 
dropwise in order to discharge the colour. Then 1 ml 
of sulphuric acid solution is added along with either 
0.5 g of solid potassium persulphate or 0.4 g solid 
ammonium persulphate. For about 30 to 40 min, gently 
boil on a preheated hot plate or till a final volume of 
10 ml is reached. Organic phosphorus compounds, such 
as AMP may take 1.5 to 2 h for complete digestion. 
Cool the solution and then dilute to 30 ml by using 
distilled water. After that add phenolphthalein indicator 
solution 0.05 ml (1 drop), and neutralize it to a faint 
pink colour by using sodium hydroxide. Makeup the 
volume up to 100 ml with distilled water. In some 
samples a precipitate is formed at this stage, but do not 
filter. Shake well for any further subdivision of sample. 
In the acidic conditions of the colorimetric reactive 
phosphorus test, the precipitate re-dissolves. 


4 VANADOMOLYBDO-PHOSPHORIC ACID 
METHOD 


4.1 Principle 


Orthophosphate reacts with ammonium molybdate 
under acid conditions to form a heteropoly acid, 
molybdophosporic acid. In the presence of vanadium, it 
changes into yellow vanadomolybdo-phosphoric acid. 
The intensity of the colour is proportional to phosphate 
concentration. 


4.2 Interference 


If the sample is heated silica and arsenate causes 
positive interferences. However arsenate, fluoride, 
thorium, bismuth, sulphide, thiosulphate, thiocyanate 
or excess molybdate causes negative interferences. 
Ferrous iron causes blue colour but this cannot be seen if 
ferrous iron is present in low concentration of 100 mg/l. 
Interference due to sulphide may be removed by using 
bromine water for oxidation. List of ions which do not 
interfere 1f present in concentrations up to 1 000 mg/l 
are aluminium ion (AI), iron ion (Fe*”), magnesium ion 
(Mg?*), calcium ion (Ca?) barium ion (Ba?) strontium 
ion (Sr?”) lithium ion (11°), sodium (Na*), potassium 
ion (K^), ammonium ion (NH*) cadmium ion (Cd?*), 
manganese ion (Мп>"), lead ion (Pb??, mercury ion 
(Hg; Hg?), tin ion (Sn?), copper ion (Cu?), nickel 
ion (№2), silver (Ag), uranium ion (049, arsinite 
ion (AsO,), bromide ion (Br), carbonate (СО,%), 
perchlorate ion (CIO^), cyanide (СХ), Iodic acid anion 
( IO, silicate (SiO,*), nitrate (NO,) , nitrite (NO, ), 
sulphate (5О,2), sulphite (SO;?), selenite, molybdate, 
pyrophosphate, teraborate,, citrate, bemzoate, oxalate, 
lactate, tartrate, formate and salicyate. 


4.2.1 Minimum Detectable Concentration 
The minimum level of concentration that can be 
detected is 200 ug/l in 1 cm spectrometer cells. 


4.3 Apparatus 


4.3.1 Spectrophotometer 


For use at 400 to 470 nm. A wavelength of 470 nm 
usually is used. The concentrations for different 
wavelengths are as specified in Table 1. 


Table 1 Concentrations for Different Wavelengths 
( Clause 4.3.1 ) 


SI No. Concentration of Phosphorous, Wavelength, 
mg/l nm 
(1) (2) 3) 
i) 1.0-5.0 400 
ii) 2.0-10.0 420 
iii) 4.0-18.0 470 


4.3.2 Acid Washed Glassware 


Use glassware that is washed with acid in order to 
determine the low concentrations of phosphorus. 
Contamination due to phosphate is common due to 
its absorption on glass surface. Use of commercial 
detergents that contains phosphate should be avoided. 
Clean the entire glassware by using hot dilute 
hydrochloric acid and after that distilled water should 
be used to rinse it well. Preferably, reserve the glassware 
for phosphate determination and after use, keep filled 


with water after washing until required. After this, acid 
treatment is required only occasionally. 


4.3.3 Filtration Apparatus 

4.3.4 Filter Paper, Whatman No 42 or equivalent. 
4.4 Reagents 

4.4.1 Phenolphthalein Indicator Aqueous Solution 


4.4.2 Hydrochloric Acid (HCl), 1 : 1 Sulphuric acid, 
perchloric acid, or nitric acid may be substituted for 
НСІ. 


4.4.3 Activated Carbon, phosphate free. Remove fine 
particle by rinsing it with distilled water. 


4.4.4 Vanadate-Molybdate Reagent 


4.4.4.1 Solution A, in 300 ml distilled water, dissolve 
25 g ammonium molybdate. 


4.4.4.2 Solution B 


By heating 300ml distilled water upto boiling, dissolve 
1.25 g ammonium meta vanadate. After that cool and 
add 330 ml concentrated hydrochloric acid. Further, 
cool solution B up to room temperature. Then solution 
A is poured into B, mixed and further diluted to 11. 


4.4.5 Standard Phosphate Solution 


In distilled water, dissolve 219.5 mg of anhydrous 
potassium di hydrogen phosphate and dilute the mixture 
to 1 000 ml (1.00 ml = 50.0 ug of orthophosphate P). 


4.5 Procedure 


4.5.1 pH Adjustment 


Ifthe pH ofthe sample is more than 10, phenolphthalein 
indicator (0.05 ml) is added to 50.0 ml of sample and 
1 + I hydrochloric acid is added so that the red colour 
is discharged. Further, the solution is diluted to 100 ml. 


4.5.2 Colour Removal 


Remove the excess of colour present in the sample 
by shaking 50 ml of sample with 200 mg of activated 
carbon for 5 min using an Erlenmeyer flask. Further, 
filter and remove carbon. Check the concentration 
of phosphate for each batch of carbon because high 
reagent blanks are produced by some batches. 


4.5.3 Colour Development 


Take 35 ml or less of the sample, which contains 
0.05 to 1.0 mg of phosphorus (P) in 50 ml flask. Now 
add vanadate-molybdate reagent (10 ml) and dilute the 
sample upto the mark by using distilled water. After 
that substitute the sample with 35 ml of the distilled 
water and after 10 min measure the absorbance at 400 to 
490 nm of wavelength, depending on sensitivity desired. 
The colour of the sample is stable for days and intensity 
Is not affected by change in room temperature. 


IS 3025 (Part 31/Sec 1) : 2022 


4.5.4 Calibration Curve 


Calibration curve is prepared by the use of suitable 
volumes of standard phosphate solution and by 
using the procedure that is given above. At least one 
standard with each set of samples should be analysed 
and the concentration of the sample should be read 
from the calibration curve for the given value of 
absorbance. 


4.6 Calculation 
Phosphorus (P), mg/l = _ 1000 


where 


m= amount of phosphorus (in 50 ml of final 
volume), in mg; and 


V = volume of sample, in ml. 
5 STANNOUS CHLORIDE METHOD 


5.1 Principle 


The molybdo-phosphoric acid is formed and 
reduced by stannous chloride and intensely coloured 
molybdenum blue is obtained. This method is 
sensitive and makes measurements down to 7 ug РЛ 
with minimum amount of interference. 


5.2 Interference 


Positive interference is caused by silica and arsenate 
only when we heat the sample. However, negative 
interferences are caused by arsenate, thorium, 
bismuth, fluoride, thiosulphate, sulphide, thiocyanate 
or excess molybdate. Ferrous iron results in blue 
colour but this does not affect the results in case 
concentration of ferrous iron is less than 100 mg/l. 
Interference due to sulphide may be removed by 
oxidation with bromine water. 


5.2.1 Minimum Detectable Concentration 


The minimum concentration that can be detected 18 
about 3ug РЛ. The sensitivity at 0.301 0 absorbance 
is about 10 ug/l for an absorbance change of 0.009. 


5.3 Apparatus 


5.3.1 Spectrophotometer 


For use at 625 nm in the measurement of 
benene-isobutanol extracts and at 690 nm, use a 
wavelength of 650 nm for aqueous solutions, with 
somewhat reduced sensitivity and precisions. 


5.4 Reagents 
5.4.1 Phenolphthalein Indicator Aqueous Solution 


5.4.2 Strong Acid Solution 


Slowly add 300 ml of concentrated sulphuric acid 
to about 600 ml of distilled water. When cool, add 
4.0 ml of concentrated nitric acid and dilute to 1 1. 


IS 3025 (Part 31/Sec 1): 2022 


5.4.3 Ammonium Molybdate Reagent I 


Dissolve 25 gm ammonium molybdate іп 175 ml 
of distilled water. After that carefully add 280 ml of 
concentrated sulphuric acid to 400 ml distilled water. 
Cool and add molybdate solution and dilute to 1 1. 


5.4.4 Stannous Chloride Reagent I 


Dissolve 2.5 gm fresh stannous chloride in 100 ml 
glycerol. Heat it on a water bath and stir it using a glass 
rod to hasten dissolution. This reagent 1s stable and does 
not require any preservatives or special storage. 


5.4.5 Standard Phosphate Solution 


Take 219.5 mg anhydrous potassium dihydrogen 
phosphate and dissolve it in distilled water. Further dilute 
it to 1 000 ml. (1.00 ml = 50.0 ug of orthophosphate P). 


5.4.6 Reagents for Extraction 


5.4.6.1 Benzene isobutanol solvent 


Mix equal volumes of isobutyl alcohol and benzene. 
CAUTION — This solvent system is highly inflammable. 


5.4.6.2 Ammonium molybdate reagent II 


Take 40.1 gm ammonium molybdate and dissolve it in 
approximately 500 ml distilled water. After that slowly 
add 396 ml ammonium molybdate reagent I. Cool and 
dilute to 11. 


5.4.6.3 Alcoholic sulphuric acid solution 


To 980 ml methyl alcohol with continuous mixing add 
20 ml concentrated sulphuric acid cautiously. 


5.4.6.4 Dilute stannous chloride reagent II 


Mix 8 ml stannous chloride reagent I and 50 ml glycerol. 
This reagent is stable and can be kept for about 6 months. 


5.5 Procedure 


5.5.1 Preliminary Sample Treatment 


To 100 ml sample that does not contains more than 
200 ug phosphorous (P) and is free from colour and 
turbidity, add phenolphthalein indicator 0.05 ml 
(1 drop). If sample turns pink, add strong acid solution 
drop by drop so as to discharge the colour. If more 
than 0.25 ml (5 drops) of acid is required, take a small 
amount of sample and dilute to 100 ml with distilled 
water after first discharging the pink colour with acid. 


5.5.2 Colour Development 


After thorough mixing after every addition, further 
add 4.0 ml molybdate reagent I and 0.5 ml (10 drops) 
stannous chloride reagent I. Intensity and rate of 
colour development depend on temperature of the final 
solution which produces about | per cent increase in 
colour intensity with each 19С temperature increase. 
Hence, hold samples, standards, and reagents within 
2 °C of one another and in the temperature range 
between 20 *C and 30 *C. 


5.5.3 Colour Measurement 


After 10 min but before 12 min, using the same 
equal intervals for all determinations, measure colour 
photometrically at 690 nm and compare with a 
calibration curve, using a distilled water blank. Light 
path lengths suitable for various concentration ranges 
are as specified in Table 2. 


Table 2 Light Path Lengths Suitable for Various 
Concentration Ranges 


( Clause 5.5.3 ) 


SI No. Approximate P Range, mg/l Light Path, cm 
0) (2) (3) 
i) 0.3-2 0.5 
ii) 0.1-1 2 
iii) 0.007- 0.2 10 


Always run a blank on distilled water and reagents. 
Because the colour first develops gradually and 
later fades, maintain equal intervals for samples and 
standards. Prepare at least one standard for each set 
of samples or once each day to conduct the tests. The 
calibration curve can deviate from a straight towards 
the higher concentrations of the 0.3 -2.0 mg/l. 


5.5.4 Extraction 


In order to increase the sensitivity and to overcome 
interferences, extraction of phosphate is done as 
follows: 


5.5.4.1 Pipette out 40 ml sample or one diluted to 
that volume, in a 125 ml separating funnel. Further 
add 50 ml benzene-isobutanol solvent and 15 ml 
molybdate reagent II. Close the funnel quickly and 
shake vigorously for exactly 15 s. In the presence 
of condensed phosphate, any delay will increase its 
conversion to orthophosphate. Remove the stopper 
and take out 25 ml of separated organic layer, using 
a pipet with safety bulb. Transfer it to a 50 ml 
volumetric flask, add 15 to 16 ml alcoholic sulphuric 
acid solution. Swirl and add 0.50 ml (10 drops) 
dilute stannous chloride reagent II. Again swirl and 
dilute it with alcoholic sulphuric acid solution. Mix 
it thoroughly and after 10 min but before 30 min 
read against the blank at a wavelength of 625 nm. 
Prepare a blank by carrying 40 ml distilled water 
by using similar procedure as used for the sample. 
Read the phosphate concentration from a calibration 
curve which is prepared by taking known phosphate 
standards by using similar procedure as used for 
samples. 


5.5.4.2 Direct procedure 
Concentration of phosphorous, mg/l = 


mg P (Approximately 104.5 ml finsl volume) * 1000 


Volume of sample in ml 


5.5.4.3 Extraction procedure 
Concentration of phosphorous, mg/l - 


mg P (Approximately 104.5 ml finsl volume) * 1000 
Volume of sample in ml 


6 ASCORBIC ACID METHOD 


6.1 Principle 


In acidic medium, ammonium  molybdate and 
antimony-potassium tartrate react with orthophosphate 
and form а  heteropoly  acid-phosphomolybdic 
acid which can be reduced to intensely coloured 
molybdenum blue by ascorbic acid. 


6.2 Interference 


Arsenates react with the molybdate reagent and gives 
a blue colour similar to that formed with phosphate. In 
low concentrations of 0.1 mg As/l arsenic can interfere 
with the determination of phosphate. At concentrations 
of 1 mg/l nitrite and hexavalent chromium interferes to 
give 3 percent lower results and 10 to 15 percent lower 
results at a concentration of about 10 mg/l. Silicates 
and sodium sulphide do not interfere at concentrations 
of 1.0 and 10 mg/l. 


6.2.1 Minimum Detectable Concentration, 
approximately 10 ug P/l. Light path lengths suitable 
for various concentration ranges are as specified in 
Table 3. 


Table 3 Light Path Lengths Suitable for Various 
Concentration Ranges 


( Clause 6.2.1 ) 


SI No. Approximate P Range, mg/l Light Path, cm 
a) (2) (3) 
i) 0.3-2 0.5 
ii) 0.15-1.3 1.0 
iii) 0.01-0.25 5.0 
6.3 Apparatus 


6.3.1 Spectrophotometer, having infrared phototube for 
use at 880 nm that can provide a light path of 2.5 cm 
or longer. 


6.3.2 Acid Washed Glassware 


For the determination of lower concentration. of 
phosphorous glassware washed with acid shall be used. 
Contamination with phosphate is common because of 
its absorption on glass surface. Commercial detergents 
containing phosphate should not be used for washing. 
Clean all glassware with hot dilute hydrochloric 
acid (НСІ) and rinse it well with distilled water. 
Preferably, keep aside the glassware only for phosphate 
determination and after use, wash it and keep it filled 
with water until required. If this is done, treatment with 
acid is needed occasionally. 


IS 3025 (Part 31/Sec 1) : 2022 


6.4 Reagents 
6.4.1 Sulfuric Acid, 5N 


Dilute 70 ml of concentrated sulphuric acid to 500 ml 
with distilled water. 


6.4.2 Antimony Potassium Tartrate Solution 


In a 500 ml volumetric flask dissolve 1.371 5 gm of 
antimony potassium tartrate in 400 ml of distilled 
water. Dilute it to the volume and store it in a 
glass-stoppered bottle. 


6.4.3 Ammonium Molybdate Solution 


Dissolve 20 gm of ammonium molybdate in 500 ml of 
distilled water and store it in a glass- stoppered bottle. 


6.4.4 Ascorbic Acid 


Dissolve 1.76 gm of ascorbic acid in 100 ml of distilled 
water. This solution is stable for about one week at 
4°C. 


6.4.5 Combined Reagent 


For 100 ml ofthe combined reagent, mix all the above 
reagents in the given proportions. Take 50 ml of 5 N 
sulphuric acid, 5 ml of antimony potassium tartrate 
solution, 15 ml of ammonium molybdate solution 
and 30 ml of ascorbic acid solution. Mix it well after 
addition of each type of reagent. АП the reagents shall 
be mixed in the order given after they reach the room 
temperature. If turbidity forms with the combined 
reagent, shake it and let it stand for a few minutes until 
turbidity disappears. The reagent is stable for upto 4 h. 


6.4.6 Stock Phosphate Solution 


Dissolve 219.5mg of anhydrous potassium dihydrogen 
phosphate in distilled water and dilute it to 1 000 ml 
(1 ml = 50.0 ug of orthophosphate P). 


6.4.7 Standard Phosphate Solution 


Dilute 50 ml of stock phosphate solution to 1 000 ml 
using distilled water (1 ml = 2.5 ир of P). 


6.5 Procedure 


6.5.1 Sample Treatment 


In a clean, dry test tube or 125 ml Erlenmeyer flask 
pipet out 50 ml of sample. To it add 0.05 ml (1 drop) 
phenolphthalein indicator. In case, a red colour develops 
add 5 N sulphuric acid solution drop by drop in order 
to just discharge the colour. Add 8.0 ml of combined 
reagent and mix it thoroughly. After 10 min but no 
more than 30 min, measure absorbance of each sample 
at a wavelength of 880 nm by using reagent blank as 
the reference solution. 


6.5.2 Correction for Turbidity or Interfering Colour 


At the higher wavelength, the natural colour of water 
generally does not interfere. In case of highly coloured 
or turbid waters, prepare a blank sample by adding all 


IS 3025 (Part 31/Sec 1): 2022 


the reagents other than antimony potassium tartrate and 
ascorbic acid to the sample. Subtract the absorbance of 
the blank from the absorbance of the sample. 


6.5.3 Preparation of Calibration Curve 


Prepare the individual calibration curves from a series 
of four up to six standards, including a blank for 
calibration, within the phosphate range, as indicated at 
6.2.1. The calibration blank solution consists of reagent 
water with the combined reagent. Plot the absorbance 
verses phosphate concentration and with each set of 
samples, test atleast one phosphate standard. 


6.6 Calculation 
mg P (in approximately 58 ml final volume) 
х 100 
mg P/l= 
ml sample 
7 PERSULFATE METHOD FOR 
SIMULTANEOUS DETERMINATION 


OF TOTAL NITROGEN AND TOTAL 
PHOSPHORUS 


7.1 Principle 


For determining total nitrogen, the oxidation of 
nitrogenous compounds must take place in an alkaline 
medium while for determining the total phosphorus, 
oxidation of phosphorus compounds must occur under 
acidic conditions. Methods for the determination oftotal 
nitrogen have used a persulphate-sodium hydroxide 
system inorder to oxidize nitrogenous compounds to 
nitrate. Accordingly, methods for the determination 
of total phosphorus have used persulphate in an acidic 
medium 


During the initial digestion stage, pH of the sample is 
7 12, that is, alkaline. In the final digestion stage, the 
sodium hydroxide is consumed which causes the pH 
to be « 2, that is, acidic. By using this wide pH range, 
the procedures allow the oxidation of both nitrogen and 
phosphorus compounds. The sample being digested is 
then analysed for nitrate and orthophosphate, yielding 
the amount of total nitrogen and total phosphorus. 


7.2 Selection of 
Measurement Methods 


Nitrate/Orthophosphate 


Using auto analyser (dual channel) which performs 
nitrate-nitrite by the cadmium reduction method and 
orthophosphate by the ascorbic acid reduction method 
and orthophosphate by the ascorbic acid reduction 
method, total nitrogen and total phosphorus can be 
measured simultaneously. Alternatively, other methods 
for orthophosphate and nitrate can be used. 


7.3 Apparatus 


7.3.1 Autoclave, should be capable of achieving a 
temperature of 120 °C for minimum of 120 min. 


7.3.2 Glass Culture Tube, 13 mm outer diameter and 
100 mm long with auto clavable caps. 


7.3.3 Autopipettor, should be capable of pipetting a 
6 ml portion. 


7.3.4 Repeating Pipettor, should be capable of 
pipetting a 1.25 ml portion. 


7.3.5 Erlenmeyer Flask, 3 000 ml. 
7.3.6 Aluminium Foil 


7.3.7 Automated Continuous Flow Instrument System 
for Nitrate and Phosphate Determination 


7.3.7.1 For nitrate determination 


An example ofa continuous-flow analytical instrument 
is as given in Fig. 1. Tubing volume and flow-rates are 
given as example only; manufacturers instruction to be 
followed. 


7.3.7.2 For phosphate determination 


An example for a kind of continuous flow analytical 
instrument consists of the interchangeable components 
are as given in the Fig. 2. A flow cell of 15 or 50 nm 
anda filter of wavelength 650 nm to 660 nm or 880 nm 
may be used. 


7.4 Reagents 


7.4.1 Deionised Water, high quality, free of phosphorus 
and nitrogen compounds. 


Prepare ammonia free water by ion-exchange or 
distillation methods. 


7.4.1.2 Ion exchange 


Ammonia-free water is prepared by passing distilled 
water through an ion exchange column containing a 
strongly acidic cation exchange resin mixed with a 
strongly basic anion exchange resin. To remove organic 
compounds which interfere with the ammonium 
determination resins are selected accordingly. Some 
anion-exchange resins tend to release ammonia. If 
ammonia is released, prepare ammonia-free water with 
a strongly acidic cation-exchange resin. Regenerate the 
column according to the manufacturer‘s instructions. 
Check ammonia-free water for the possibility of a high 
blank value. 


7.4.1.3 Distillation 


The traces of ammonia in distilled water are eliminated 
by adding 0.1 ml concentrated sulphuric acid to distilled 
water and redistilling. Alternatively, treat distilled water 
with sufficient bromine or chlorine water to produce a 
free halogen residual of 2 to 5 mg/l and redistill after 
standing at least 1 h. Discard the first 100 ml of the 
distillate. Check redistilled water for the possibility of 
a high blank. 


It is very difficult to store ammonia-free water in 
the laboratory without contamination from gaseous 
ammonia. However, If storage is necessary, store in 
a tightly stoppered glass container to which is added 
about 10 gm 1on exchange resin (preferably strongly 
acidic catio exchange resin)/l ammonia free water. If 
a high blank value is produced , replace the resin or 
prepare fresh ammonia free water. 


Use ammonia free distilled water for preparing all 
reagents, rinsing and sample dilution. 


7.4.2 Sodium Hydroxide, 3 N 


Dissolve about 120 gm low nitrogen sodium hydroxide 
in about 800 ml deionized water taken in a 1 000 ml 
volumetric flask. Cool and dilute to volume. 


7.4.3 Oxidizing Reagent 


In 500 ml deionised water dissolve 64 gm low nitrogen 
(«0.001 percent N ) potassium per sulphate. If necessary 
use low heat. Add 80 ml of 3 N sodium hydroxide 
prepared from low -nitrogen sodium hydroxide and 
dilute to 1 000 ml. Store the reagent prepared in a 
brown bottle at room temperature. 


7.4.4 Reagents for Determining Nitrate and Nitrite 


7.4.4.1 Reagent water 


Ammonia free distilled water 1s used for preparing all 
reagents, rinsing and sample dilution. 


7.4.4.2 Copper sulphate solution 


In 500 ml reagent water, dissolve 20 g copper sulphate 
and dilute to 1 1 with reagent water. This solution 18 
stable for 1 year. 


7.4.4.3 Wash solution, use reagent water. 


7.4.4.4 Copper-cadmium (Cd) granules 


Wash 25 gm new or used 20-100 mesh Cd granules 
with 6 M hydrochloric acid and rinse with water. For 
5 min swirl Cd with 100 ml 2 percent copper sulphate 
solution until blue colour partially fades. Decant 
and repeat with fresh copper sulphate until a brown 
colloidal precipitate begins to develop. Gently flush 
with ammonium chloride-ethylene diamine tetraacetic 
acid (EDTA) solution to remove all precipitated copper. 
Store activated Cd covered with dilute ammonium 
chloride-EDTA solution. 


7.4.4.5 Colour reagent 


To 800 ml reagent water, add 100 ml 85 per cent 
phosphoric acid and 10 gm sulphanilamide. After 
dissolving sulphanilamide completely, add 1gm NED. 
Mix to dissolve, then dilute to 1 litre with water. 
Solution is stable for about a month when stored in an 
amber bottle in a refrigerator. Discard if the solution is 
highly coloured or dark or if a precipitate forms. 


IS 3025 (Part 31/Sec 1) : 2022 


7.4.4.6 Ammonium chloride-EDTA solution 


Dissolve 13 gm ammonium chloride and 1.7 gm 
disodium ethylene di amine tetra-acetate to 900 ml 
reagent water. Adjust to pH 8.5 with concentrate 
ammonium hydroxide and dilute to 1 | with reagent 
water. This solution is stable for 1 year. 


Use low heat EDTA solution to 500 ml with water. Use 


this reagent as a cadmium-reduction-column storage 
solution. 


7.4.4.8 Hydrochloric acid, 6 M 
Carefully add 500 ml concentrated hydrochloric acid to 


400 ml, reagent water. Dilute tol | with reagent water. 
This solution is stable for 1 year. 


7.4.4.9 Stock nitrate solution A 


At 103 *C-105 “С dry potassium nitrate in an oven for 
24 h. Dissolve 0.7218 gm (+ 0.000 5 gm) in water and 
dilute to 100 ml (1ml = 100 ug of nitrate). Preserve 
with 2 ml chloroform/l. This solution is stable for at 
least 6 months. 


7.4.4.10 Stock nitrate solution B 


Purchase from a commercial source different from 
stock nitrate solution A. 


7.4.4.11 Intermediate nitrate solution А 


Dilute 100 ml stock nitrate solution to 1 000 ml 
with water (Iml = 10 ug nitrate М). Preserve with 
2 ml chloroform/l. This solution is stable for at least 
6 months. 


7.4.5 Reagents for Determining Phosphorus 


7.4.5.1 Antimony potassium tartrate solution 


Dissolve 0.3 g antimony potassium tartrate in 
approximately 50 ml distilled water and dilute to 
100 ml with reagent water. Store in 4 *C in a dark, glass 
stoppered bottle. 


7.4.5.2 Ammonium molybdate solution 


Dissolve 4 g ammonium molybdate in 100 ml distilled 
water. Store in plastic bottle at 4 °C. 


7.4.5.3 Ascorbic acid 


Dissolve 1.76 gm ascorbic acid in 100 ml distilled 
water. This solution is stable for about 1 week at 4 ?C. 


7.4.5.4 Combined reagent 


Mix the above reagents in the following proportions for 
100 ml of the combined reagent, 50 ml 5 N sulphuric 
acid, 5 ml antimony potassium tartrate solution, 15 ml 
ammonium molybdate solution and 30 ml ascorbic 
acid solution. Mix after addition of each reagent. Let 
all reagents reach room temperature before they are 
mixed and mix in the order given, If turbidity forms 
in the combined reagent, shake and let stand for a few 


IS 3025 (Part 31/Sec 1): 2022 


minutes until turbidity disappears before proceeding. 
The reagent is stable for 4 h. 


7.4.5.5 Dilute sulphuric acid solution 


Slowly add 140 ml concentrated sulphuric acid to 
600 ml distilled water. When cool dilute to 11. 


7.4.5.6 Ammonium persulphate, crystalline 
7.4.5.7 Phenolphthalein indicator aqueous solution 


7.4.5.8 Stock phosphate solution 


Dissolve 439.3 mg anhydrous potassium di hydrogen 
phosphate dried for 1 h at 105 ?C, in distilled water and 
dilute to 1 000 ml (1.00 ml 7100.0 ug of phosphorus). 


7.4.5.9 Intermediate phosphate solution 


Dilute 100 ml stock phosphate solution to 1 000 ml 
with distilled water (1.0 ml = 10.0 ug of phosphorus). 


7.4.5.10 Standard phosphate solution 


Prepare a suitable series of standards by diluting 
appropriate volumes of intermediate phosphate 
solution. 


7.4.6 Nicotinic Acid P-toluene Sulfonate Stock and 
Working Standards 


For 24 h dry nicotinic acid p-toluene sulfonate in an 
oven at a temperature of 150 °C. Dissolve about 2.108 
4 gm of it in deionized water and dilute to 100 ml 
(1 ml = 1 mg of nitrogen). Dilute 2 ml of stock solution 
to 1 000 ml, to prepare a working standard (Iml=2 ug 
of nitrogen). 


7.4.7 Adenosine Triphosphate Stock and Working 
Standards 


In deionized water dissolve 0.651 4 gm adenosine 
triphosphate and dilute it to 100 ml (1ml = 0.1 mg of 
phosphorus). To prepare a working standard, dilute 
20 ml of stock solution to 1 000 ml (1ml = 2 ug of 
phosphorus). Dilute 1 ml stock solution to 1 000 ml, to 
prepare a low range working standard (1ml = 0.1 ug of 
phosphorus). 


7.5 Procedure 


7.5.1 Calibration Curve 


Prepare at least 5 standards over the desired calibration 
ranges such that a stock calibration standard containing 
both nitrate and orthophosphate. Treat the standards 
in the same manner just like samples. In calibration 
curves include blanks. 


7.5.2 Sample Preparation 


If required, dilute the sample with de-ionized water 
so that the expected concentrations of nitrogen and 
phosphorus fall within the limit of the calibration 
standards. This digestion method cannot be used for 
samples that are preserved with acid for determination. 


7.5.3 Digestion Check Standards 


Analyse the quality control standards that contains 
organic nitrogen and phosphorus on each analytical 
run by using the nicotinic acid p-toluenesulfonate 
standard (for nitrogen) and adenosine triphosphate 
standard (for phosphorus). These standards provide 
the reference checks on the calibration and test the 
ability of the digestion. 


7.5.4 Digestion 


Pipet out 6 ml of sample or standard in to the culture 
tubes. Further add 1.25 ml oxidizing reagent to each 
tube using a repeating pipet or and cover the tubes by 
using loose fitting caps. Prepare an auto analyser wash 
water in an Erlenmeyer flask by adding oxidation 
reagent to deionized water in the same ratio as 1t was 
added to the samples. Cover the flask by using a foil. 
Autoclave the samples and wash water for 55 min at 
120 9С. Cool to room temperature. Add about 0.05 
ml of 3 N NaOH to each tube before proceeding to 
nitrate, nitrite and phosphate analysis. Shake to mix. 
Add same proportion of 3 N NaOH to digested wash 
water. 


7.5.5 Final Nitrate and Nitrite Measurement 


Use the automated cadmium reduction method to find 
out the concentration of nitrate-nitrite after digestion. 
Other nitrate analysis methods may be applicable for 
this. 


7.5.6 Final Phosphate Measurement 


Use the automated ascorbic acid reduction method 
to find out the concentration of phosphate after 
digestion. Other phosphate analysis methods may be 
applicable. 


7.6 Calculation 


Prepare standard curves for nitrogen and phosphorus 
by plotting the instrument response of standards 
against the standard concentrations. Compute the 
concentrations of nitrogen and phosphorus by 
comparing the response ofthe sample with the standard 
curve. Where required, multiply the concentration of 
the sample by the appropriate dilution factor to find 
out the final concentration. 


IS 3025 (Part 31/Sec 1): 2022
